paper_title: Effects of different plasma substitutes on blood coagulation: A comparative review
target_conclusion: In patients with increased risk of bleeding, rapidly degradable HES 200/0.5/6 and gelatin-based plasma expanders may be preferred over slowly degradable HES or dextran

nodes.text: Dextran: pronounced anticoagulant effects. Impairs platelet function via platelet coating. Reduces vWF/FVIII activity (vWF:RCo decreased 23% at 24h, FVIII:C decreased 40% at 24h in volunteers). Impairs fibrin polymerization (40% reduction in maximum rate of polymerization). Associated with increased postoperative blood loss (8 of 11 comparative studies showed more blood loss; meta-analysis: 231ml mean increase in CABG).

HES: effects on coagulation depend on MW, C2/C6 ratio, and degree of substitution. High MW HES (hetastarch 450/0.7): impairs coagulation most, increases blood loss in CABG. Medium MW slowly degradable (HES 200/0.62, HES 200/0.5/13): impair coagulation after repeated administration. Medium MW rapidly degradable (HES 200/0.5/6, pentastarch): fewer hemostatic effects, not associated with increased blood loss. Low MW (HES 70/0.5): under investigation, minimal effects. FVIII:C decreased with all HES types, most with slowly degradable. vWF decreased most with hetastarch. Fibrin polymerization impaired by high MW and slowly degradable HES. Platelet effects: conflicting data, some studies show decreased aggregation with high MW, fewer effects with low MW.

Gelatin: least adverse effect on coagulation. Does not consistently decrease FVIII or vWF. Fibrin polymerization not affected. Not associated with increased postoperative blood loss in any of 6 comparative studies. Plasmavolume expander (Haemaccel) showed no significant effect on blood loss vs Ringer's lactate.

Boldt et al. [61] and Rackow et al. [119] did not find significant differences in platelet function between HES and albumin in patients after cardiac surgery and in patients with sepsis, respectively. Boldt 1996: HES 200/0.5 vs 20% albumin in 56 ICU patients (28 trauma, 28 sepsis), 5-day infusion, aggregometry with ADP/collagen/epinephrine — no significant difference found.

nodes.text: HES and platelet function synthesis: In vivo, decreased platelet aggregation reported with hetastarch in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass. Boldt et al. [61] and Rackow et al. [119] did not find significant differences in platelet function between HES and albumin. Platelet effects of HES appear to be related to MW, C2/C6 ratio, dose, and in vivo vs in vitro conditions. General mechanism: HES may coat platelets, interfere with GPIb and GPIIb/IIIa receptor function, and alter vWF-mediated adhesion.

nodes.text: MW/substitution mechanism synthesis: All synthetic colloids can induce decrease of vWF and FVIII:C. Degree of impairment correlates with MW, C2/C6 ratio, and rate of elimination. Rapidly degradable HES (200/0.5/6) and gelatin appear to have fewest hemostatic effects based on laboratory and clinical data. Slowly degradable HES (200/0.62, 200/0.5/13) impair coagulation after repeated doses due to plasma accumulation.

Gelatin vs HES comparison: Gelatin does not consistently decrease FVIII or vWF, does not impair fibrin polymerization, and is not associated with increased blood loss. HES effects are formulation-dependent. In comparative studies, gelatin shows fewer hemostatic effects than slowly degradable HES, and comparable or fewer effects than rapidly degradable HES.

nodes.text: In patients with increased risk of bleeding, rapidly degradable HES 200/0.5/6 and gelatin-based plasma expanders may be preferred over slowly degradable HES or dextran. This claim is supported by: (1) Boldt & Rackow finding no platelet function difference for HES 200/0.5 vs albumin, (2) laboratory data showing fewer coagulation effects of rapidly degradable HES, (3) gelatin's minimal hemostatic impact.
Blood coagulation is most impaired by dextran and high MW or slowly degradable HES, both associated with increased postoperative blood loss.
The most important determinant of hemostatic safety of plasma substitutes is the rate of degradation.

nodes.text: The same colloid preferences apply to patients with von Willebrand disease. All artificial colloids could potentially induce increased bleeding tendency after infusion of very large volumes.

nodes.text: All colloids except albumin can induce specific decreases of vWF and FVIII:C. Hemodilution alone does not explain the observed changes; specific interactions with coagulation factors are involved.
